title: Screenshots Are Bad for Your Memory — Here's Why
paragraphs: Many of us take screenshots of things we want to remember, such as recipes, directions or interesting articles. However, a new study suggests that this habit may actually make us more likely to forget the information.

The study, titled "Digital amnesia: The aftermath of a screenshot," was carried out by psychologists at Binghamton University in New York, including lead author Sophia Fabrizio and Professor Deanne Westerman. It was published in the journal Memory & Cognition in 2026.

The researchers conducted seven experiments in which participants looked at works of art and sometimes captured images of them, before being tested on how well they remembered the artworks. In some experiments, participants also had to solve math problems. Across all of the experiments, taking screenshots did not provide any clear benefit to memory. Instead, participants remembered the information less well.

This is an example of what researchers call the "photo-taking impairment effect." Interestingly, earlier research found that photos taken automatically by a camera worn on the body did not harm memory. This suggests that it is the act of choosing to take a picture that matters.

Why might this happen? One possible explanation is that taking a picture divides our attention. However, the researchers believe this is unlikely to be the main cause, because memory was still impaired even when participants had extra time or the task was easier. Another explanation is "cognitive offloading," which means that when we know information is stored somewhere else, we make less effort to remember it ourselves. Surprisingly, memory remained impaired even when participants knew their images would be deleted. The researchers are also testing whether taking pictures causes people to become mentally disconnected from what they are experiencing.
This matters because people take a lot of photos. According to Fabrizio, people take around 20 photos a day on average, and the average smartphone stores about 2,000 images.

However, screenshots are not always harmful. The researchers suggest that taking a small number of intentional screenshots and reviewing them later can actually support memory. As Fabrizio explained, screenshots are unlikely to help unless people actively review them. Writing notes by hand may also help, because organizing information requires more mental effort, which can strengthen memory.
